newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: French, Malaysians contest Ivorian phone deal.
newsitem.headline: French, Malaysians contest Ivorian phone deal.

text.p: French and Malaysian bidders look set to battle for the takeover of Ivory Coast's phone monopoly CI-TELCOM, after major U.S. carriers backed away from the debt-ridden network, industry sources said on Wednesday.

They said state-owned France-Telecom and Telecom Malaysia were among three foreign firms short-listed last week to submit detailed bids for CI-TELCOM next month. The winner is expected to be picked in December as operator, with a 51 percent stake.
France-Telecom said earlier it bid for the network through a local subsidiary including Ivorian commodities giant, SIFCOM.
A third bidder, Africa Bell, a consortium including Ivorian and U.S. entities, will vie with the French and Malaysians who are on familiar ground in the region.
"France-Telecom was one of the three companies selected to submit detailed bids on November 25," France-Telecom's Ivory Coast representative Henri Neuville told Reuters.

Officials of the government's privatisation committee and Paris-based lead manager Rothschild and Co confirmed that an operator for CI-TELCOM would be decided after next month's submissions. They declined to comment on the short-list.

France-Telecom has historical ties to the former French colony and is a major provider of international circuits and technical services to CI-TELCOM. Its subsidiary, France Cable Radio, holds a 70 percent stake in one of three cellular telephone companies preparing to start services in Ivory Coast.
It is also owed a substantial amount of money by CI-TELCOM -- the bulk of the company's total debt estimated independently at hundreds of millions of dollars.
Neuville said the debt could add weight to France-Telecom's bid. "I think the debt will be an important factor," he said.
The Malaysians are counting on their experience in running the privatised telephone company in Guinea for which they paid $45 million last Decemebr.
If they clinch the Ivorian deal, CI-TELCOM is likely to be refurbished with Japanese equipment, replacing the largely French infrastructure now creaking, industry sources said.

U.S. industry sources said major U.S. carriers, notably AT&T and MCI Communications Corp who have international circuits into Ivory Coast showed initial interest in the bid but eventually backed out mainly because of the cost.
"I think they reckoned that it was more profitable for them to stay in the business of providing circuits," one said.
The Ivorian government, which is privatising state-owned companies in a drive to attract foreign investment, is selling off 51 percent of its holding in CI-TELCOM to a strategic partner.
It will retain 35 percent for itself and two percent for staff while selling off the remaining shares to the public.
Estimates of the total value of CI-TELCOM range from $200 million to $350 million. But the government has said it is worried about its huge debt and negative working capital.
Managing Director Brou N'Gbla said in an interview published on Wednesday CI-TELCOM needed 600 billion CFA ($1.1 billion) in investment to provide telephone lines for 100,000 new subscribers.

"I think the problem here is the cost. You buy the shares but you have to invest heavily," one industry analysts said. "You are gambling on debt, huge telephone penetration and network upgrade. Who knows if they are going to have strong growth to pay for all that investment?"
